title: Freelance Case Study Kit
description: Turn finished projects into case studies that win the next client: a fill-in template, a complete worked example, twelve client interview questions, five feedback, permission and approval emails, a before-and-after results tracker, and a checklist for using case studies on your site, in proposals and in outreach.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Case Study Kit

Turn finished projects into case studies that win the next client. A good
case study shows a prospect someone like them, a problem like theirs, and
what changed when they hired you. This kit takes you from "I should write
that up some day" to a published case study in about two hours.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| case-study-template.md | A fill-in-the-blanks structure for one case study | 60-90 min per case study |
| worked-example.md | A complete case study written with the template, so you can see the finished shape | 10 min read |
| client-interview-questions.md | Twelve questions for a short call that gets you the story and the results | 20-minute call |
| permission-and-feedback-emails.md | Emails to ask for feedback, permission to publish, and a review of your draft | Copy as needed |
| results-tracker.csv | Capture before-and-after numbers while the project runs, with example rows | 5 min per project |
| portfolio-page-checklist.md | How to lay out and use case studies on your site, in proposals and in outreach | 30 min, once |

## How to use it

1. **Start tracking now.** Add every current project to results-tracker.csv
   and note the "before" numbers today. Results are much easier to show
   when you captured the starting point.
2. **Ask at the right moment.** When a project wraps up and the client is
   happy, send the feedback email from permission-and-feedback-emails.md.
3. **Have a short call.** Use client-interview-questions.md. Twenty
   minutes is enough; the client's own words are the best material you'll
   get.
4. **Write it up.** Fill in case-study-template.md. Look at worked-example.md
   if you get stuck on a section.
5. **Get approval.** Send the draft for the client's review before
   publishing, using the approval email. Never publish a client's name,
   numbers or words without their clear permission.
6. **Use it everywhere.** Follow portfolio-page-checklist.md to put the case
   study on your site, in proposals and in your outreach emails.

## Honesty rules

Case studies only work if prospects trust them.

- Only use real projects, real results and the client's actual words.
- Only quote a client who has agreed to be quoted, in the form they
  approved.
- If you can't share a client's name or numbers, say so ("a regional
  accountancy firm", "traffic more than doubled") rather than inventing
  details.
- Don't claim credit for results caused by other things. If sales went
  up during a big ad campaign, say so.

The example case study in this kit is fictional and marked as such. It is
there to show the structure, not to be copied.
files.case-study-template.md:
# Case study template

Copy this file for each case study. Replace everything in [square
brackets]. Delete the guidance notes (the lines starting with "Note:")
before publishing. Aim for 400-700 words in total: long enough to be
convincing, short enough to be read.

---

## Title

[Result] for [type of client]

Note: lead with the outcome, not the service. "Booked out three months
ahead: a new website for a physiotherapy clinic" beats "Website design
for ABC Physio". If you can't share a number, use a clear plain result:
"A menu people can actually read on their phones".

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Client | [Name, or a description if anonymous: "a two-person bakery"] |
| Industry | [Industry] |
| What I did | [Service, in client words: "new website", not "full-stack build"] |
| Timeline | [Length of project] |
| Key result | [The single most important outcome, with a number if you have one] |

Note: many readers will only read this box. Make it work on its own.

## The situation

[Two to four sentences. Who is the client, what were they trying to do,
and what was getting in the way? Describe the problem the way the client
would, so prospects with the same problem recognise themselves.]

Note: include one concrete detail that shows the problem was real ("they
were taking bookings by phone only, and missing calls during
appointments").

## Why it mattered

[One or two sentences on the cost of the problem: lost time, lost
customers, stress, missed opportunities.]

## What I did

[Three to five short points or a short paragraph. Focus on the decisions
you made and why, not a list of every task.]

- [Step or decision one, and the reason for it]
- [Step or decision two, and the reason for it]
- [Step or decision three, and the reason for it]

Note: this is where you show how you think. "I suggested cutting the site
from twelve pages to five, because their customers only ever asked about
three things" says more than "designed a five-page site".

## The result

[The outcomes, as specific as you can honestly make them. Before and
after numbers from results-tracker.csv, time saved, things the client can
now do. If numbers are confidential, describe the change in plain words.]

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| [Measure] | [Before] | [After] |
| [Measure] | [Before] | [After] |

[If other things also contributed, say so in one sentence.]

## In the client's words

"[A short quote from the interview, approved by the client.]"

[Name, role, organisation, as approved; or "Owner, regional accountancy
firm" if anonymous]

Note: only include this section if the client has approved the exact
wording. If you don't have an approved quote, leave the section out.

## Is this you?

[One or two sentences aimed at the next client: "If you run a small
clinic and your booking system is costing you calls, I can help." Then
your call to action: how to get in touch or what to do next.]

---

## Before you publish

    [ ] The title leads with the result
    [ ] The "at a glance" box makes sense on its own
    [ ] Every number is real and from the tracker or the client
    [ ] Other contributing factors are mentioned
    [ ] The quote is in the exact wording the client approved
    [ ] The client has approved the whole draft in writing
    [ ] Confidential details are removed or anonymised
    [ ] It ends with a clear next step for the reader
files.client-interview-questions.md:
# Client interview: twelve questions in twenty minutes

A short call with your client gives you the two things you can't write
yourself: the problem in their words, and what changed for them. Book it
within two weeks of the project ending, while it's still fresh.

## Before the call

- Send the questions in advance (the feedback email in
  permission-and-feedback-emails.md does this), so nothing feels like a
  surprise.
- Ask if you may record the call or take notes, and explain it's only so
  you can quote them accurately. Make it easy to say no.
- Open results-tracker.csv and check what numbers you already have.
- Tell them nothing will be published without their approval of the
  final wording.

## The questions

Ask them in this order. Let silences run; the best answers often come
after a pause. If an answer is general, ask "can you give me an example?"

### Before (the situation)

1. What was going on in your business before we started working together?
2. What made you decide to do something about it at that point?
3. What had you already tried, if anything?
4. What were you most worried about before starting?

### During (working together)

5. Why did you choose to work with me rather than another option?
6. Was there a moment in the project that stood out, good or bad?
7. Is there anything you'd want me to do differently next time?

Question 7 matters. It shows you take feedback seriously, and the answers
help you improve. You won't publish it unless they want you to.

### After (the result)

8. What's different now, day to day?
9. Have you noticed any change in numbers? (bookings, sales, enquiries,
   time spent, anything you track)
10. Has anyone else, like customers, staff or partners, commented on it?

### Wrapping up

11. If a friend in your position asked you about working with me, what
    would you tell them?
12. Is there anything I haven't asked that you'd like to mention?

## After the call

Within a day:

1. Write down the strongest three or four phrases they used, word for
   word. Mark which ones you'd like to quote.
2. Add any new numbers to results-tracker.csv.
3. Send a thank-you note.
4. Draft the case study using case-study-template.md, then send it for
   approval with the approval email.

## Tips

- **Use their words for the problem.** Prospects search for and recognise
  problems in their own language, not in yours.
- **Don't lead.** "Did the new site make things easier?" invites a polite
  yes. "What's different now?" gets a real answer.
- **Don't fix quotes into marketing copy.** Light tidying for grammar is
  fine if the client approves it; changing the meaning is not.
- **Keep it short.** If you promised twenty minutes, finish in twenty.
files.permission-and-feedback-emails.md:
# Feedback, permission and approval emails

Five emails covering the whole process, from asking for feedback to
getting a final yes. Replace everything in [square brackets] and adjust
the tone to match how you normally write to the client.

---

## 1. Asking for feedback and a short call

Send when the project is finished and the client is happy, usually within
a week of the final delivery or invoice being paid.

> Subject: A quick favour, and some feedback on [project]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Now that [project] is finished, I'd really value twenty minutes of your
> time to hear how it went: what worked, and what I could do better.
>
> With your permission, I'd also like to write up the project as a short
> case study for my website. Nothing would be published without you
> seeing and approving the final wording, and I can leave out your name
> or any numbers you'd rather keep private.
>
> The questions I'd ask are below, so you can see what's involved.
> Would [day/time] or [day/time] suit you?
>
> [Paste the questions from client-interview-questions.md]
>
> Thanks either way,
> [Your name]

---

## 2. If they'd prefer to write rather than talk

> Subject: Re: A quick favour
>
> No problem at all. If it's easier, just reply with a few lines on
> these four questions, whenever you have time:
>
> 1. What was going on before we started?
> 2. Why did you decide to work with me?
> 3. What's different now?
> 4. Is there anything I could have done better?
>
> Short answers are perfect.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 3. Asking for permission to publish

Use when they've given feedback but you haven't yet asked about
publishing, or when you want explicit permission for specific details.

> Subject: May I share [project] as a case study?
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks again for the kind feedback on [project]. I'd like to share the
> project on my website and occasionally in proposals to similar
> businesses.
>
> Could you let me know which of these you're comfortable with?
>
> - Using your business name: yes / no
> - Using your name and role: yes / no
> - Sharing the numbers we discussed ([list numbers]): yes / no
> - Quoting you: yes / no
> - Using images of the work: yes / no
>
> Anything you say no to, I'll leave out or describe generally (for
> example, "a two-person clinic"). You'll see the full draft before
> anything goes live.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 4. Sending the draft for approval

> Subject: Draft case study for your approval
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Here's the draft case study about [project]. [Attach or paste it.]
>
> Please check in particular:
>
> - the quote from you, which is [exact quote]
> - the numbers: [list numbers]
> - anything you'd rather I didn't mention
>
> Edit anything you like. I'll only publish once you've replied to say
> you're happy with it.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 5. Thank-you and confirmation

> Subject: Thank you, it's live
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for approving the case study. It's now on my site at [address].
>
> If you ever want anything changed or taken down, just let me know and
> I'll do it straight away.
>
> [Your name]

---

## Keeping a record

Save the client's written approval (the email where they say yes) with
the project files. If the client later asks for a change or removal, act
on it promptly, and update your site, proposals and any saved outreach
templates that use the case study.
files.portfolio-page-checklist.md:
# Using case studies: site, proposals and outreach

A case study that sits on a page nobody visits doesn't win work. This
checklist covers where to put each case study and how to present it.

## On your website

### The portfolio or work page

- Show three to six case studies, not every project you've done. Choose
  the ones closest to the clients you want more of.
- Order them by relevance to your ideal client, not by date.
- For each one, show a card with: the result-led title, the type of
  client, one image or a short line about the work, and a link to the
  full case study.
- Let visitors filter or group by client type if you serve more than
  one kind of client ("clinics", "shops", "professional services").

### Each case study page

    [ ] Result-led title at the top
    [ ] "At a glance" box near the top
    [ ] One or two images of the work, if the client approved them
    [ ] Headings that match the template, so the page is easy to scan
    [ ] Approved client quote, if you have one
    [ ] A clear next step at the end: contact, book a call, or reply
    [ ] A link to one or two related case studies
    [ ] Reads well on a phone

### Elsewhere on your site

- Put the single strongest result on your homepage, near the top, with a
  link to the full case study.
- On each service page, link the case study that best shows that
  service.
- On your contact page, a one-line reminder of a result can help
  someone who is nearly ready to get in touch.

## In proposals

- Include one or two case studies that match the prospect's situation.
  One close match beats five loose ones.
- Use a short version: title, the "at a glance" box and two sentences of
  result, with a link to the full version.
- Mention the match explicitly: "This is the closest project to yours,
  because they also [shared problem]."

## In outreach and follow-ups

- In a first email to a new prospect, one sentence and a link is enough:
  "I recently helped a two-person clinic cut missed calls by about two
  thirds; the write-up is here: [link]."
- In a follow-up after no reply, a relevant case study gives you a
  genuine reason to write again.
- With past clients, sharing a new case study is a friendly way to stay
  in touch, and it often prompts referrals.

## Keeping it fresh

- Add one new case study every two to three months, or whenever you
  finish a project that shows something new.
- Review the set every six months. Retire older ones that no longer
  match the work you want.
- If a client asks for a case study to be changed or removed, do it
  promptly everywhere you've used it: site, proposals and saved email
  templates.

## A simple schedule

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Project start | Add the project to results-tracker.csv with before numbers |
| Project end | Send feedback email |
| Within 2 weeks | Interview call |
| Within 3 weeks | Draft and send for approval |
| 4-8 weeks after end | Update after numbers and publish |
| Every 6 months | Review and retire old case studies |

files.worked-example.md:
# Worked example: a finished case study

This is a fictional example written with case-study-template.md. The
client, numbers and project are invented to show the structure and tone.
Do not publish it or reuse its numbers; write your own from real
projects.

The quote section is shown as a placeholder on purpose. In a real case
study it would contain the client's own approved words.

---

## From missed calls to online bookings: a website for a two-person physio clinic

| | |
|---|---|
| Client | Example Physio, a two-practitioner clinic (fictional) |
| Industry | Health and wellbeing |
| What I did | New five-page website with online booking |
| Timeline | Five weeks |
| Key result | Phone calls during appointments fell from about 15 a week to about 4 |

## The situation

Example Physio took every booking by phone. Both practitioners spend most
of the day with patients, so calls went to voicemail, and many callers
never left a message. Their existing website was twelve pages long, hard
to read on a phone, and didn't say clearly which conditions they treat
or what a first appointment costs.

## Why it mattered

Every missed call was a potential new patient who might book elsewhere.
Returning calls at the end of the day also added about an hour of unpaid
work for the owners, most evenings.

## What I did

- **Cut the site to five pages.** Their records showed new patients asked
  about three things: what they treat, prices, and parking. I built the
  site around those three questions.
- **Added online booking** using the booking tool they already paid for
  but hadn't set up, so there was no new monthly cost.
- **Put prices on the homepage.** The owners were nervous about this. We
  agreed to try it for a month; they kept it.
- **Wrote for phones first.** Most visitors arrived on a phone, so every
  page was designed to work with a thumb, with the booking button always
  in view.

## The result

| Measure | Before | After (first two months) |
|---|---|---|
| Calls during appointments | About 15 a week | About 4 a week |
| New bookings made online | 0 | 38 |
| Evening time returning calls | About 1 hour a day | About 15 minutes a day |

The clinic also started a small local leaflet campaign in the second
month, which likely contributed to some of the online bookings.

## In the client's words

"[Approved quote from the client interview would go here.]"

[Name, role, Example Physio, as approved]

## Is this you?

If you run a small clinic or practice and the phone is getting in the way
of your work, I'd be glad to have a look at your site. Send me a link and
I'll reply with three things I'd change first.

---

## Why this example works

- The title leads with the result and names the type of client, so a
  similar business recognises itself straight away.
- The "at a glance" box gives the whole story in five lines.
- The situation uses a concrete detail (calls going to voicemail) rather
  than a vague claim ("they needed a better online presence").
- "What I did" explains reasons, which shows judgement, not just tasks.
- The results table uses before and after numbers and admits another
  factor (the leaflet campaign).
- It ends with a specific, low-effort next step for the reader.
